intro: Every project below was built for EN.605.256 Modern Software Concepts in Python. They are not thirteen unrelated exercises: Module 2 scrapes 30,000 graduate admissions records from The Grad Cafe, and almost everything after it works on that same dataset, through a relational database, a tested and hardened web application, a container stack, AWS, statistics, clustering, experiment tracking, and finally two neural networks. Each block links to its folder in the course repository.

projects.title: Personal Flask Website
projects.overview: A three-page personal site built with Flask, using an application factory and one blueprint per page. Home, Contact, and Projects share a single Jinja layout with custom CSS.
projects.learned: Blueprints and template inheritance turned what would have been three near-identical HTML files into one layout plus three small route modules, which was the first time structure paid off for me instead of just adding files.
projects.highlight: Now renders this portfolio page from JSON rather than hard-coded HTML

projects.title: Web Scraping with Local LLM Cleaning
projects.overview: Scrapes graduate admissions results from The Grad Cafe with Selenium and BeautifulSoup, then standardizes the messy free-text program and university fields using a locally hosted TinyLlama model. The output is a structured JSON dataset of 30,000 applicant entries that every later module builds on.
projects.learned: Checking robots.txt and holding a two second delay per page taught me that the real constraints on scraping are etiquette and rate limits rather than parsing, and that a small local model can clean text no regular expression could.
projects.highlight: 30,000 entries scraped and standardized by a self-hosted model, no external API

projects.title: PostgreSQL and SQL Analysis
projects.overview: Loads the 30,000-entry dataset into a local PostgreSQL database and answers eleven analytical questions with SQL, presenting the results on a dynamic Flask page with a live data refresh button.
projects.learned: Running the same query against the raw program field and the cleaned one showed the value of Module 2 in a single number: it returned nothing on the raw text and 28 rows on the standardized field.
projects.highlight: 11 SQL questions; the university query returns 0 rows raw against 28 cleaned

projects.title: Testing and Documentation
projects.overview: Adds a complete pytest suite at 100% branch coverage plus Sphinx developer documentation to the Grad Cafe Flask application, with GitHub Actions running the suite against a PostgreSQL service on every push.
projects.learned: Getting to 100% coverage forced me to refactor toward an application factory and injected dependencies, so the tests ended up changing the design rather than just checking it.
projects.highlight: 41 tests over 175 statements at 100% coverage, docs published to Read the Docs

projects.title: Software Assurance and Secure SQL
projects.overview: Hardens the application behind a Pylint 10.00/10 gate, rewrites every query using psycopg's sql.SQL composition instead of string building, and adds a least-privilege database user, a dependency graph, and Snyk supply-chain scanning.
projects.learned: Composing SQL with sql.Identifier and sql.Literal makes injection structurally impossible instead of merely unlikely, which is a better kind of safety than remembering to escape every input.
projects.highlight: 10.00/10 with no messages silenced, alongside 100% test coverage

projects.title: Dockerized Microservices
projects.overview: Refactors the single Flask application into a four-service stack that runs anywhere through Docker Compose: web, worker, PostgreSQL, and RabbitMQ. Button clicks publish a task to the broker and a background worker consumes it, so no request ever waits on a scrape.
projects.learned: Putting a message broker between the web app and the work meant a button could return immediately, and it was the first time I designed for failure by making ingestion idempotent and watermarked so a repeated task could not double-insert.
projects.highlight: 4 services published to Docker Hub, running as a non-root user

projects.title: AWS Cloud Deployment
projects.overview: Two cloud deliverables: pulling the dataset from a private S3 bucket into a SageMaker notebook with boto3, and deploying the Module 6 Compose stack onto an EC2 instance behind a locked-down security group.
projects.learned: Relying on an IAM execution role rather than access keys meant no credential ever had to enter the repository, and narrowing the security group to a single IP made me think about exposure instead of just getting the port open.
projects.highlight: Arm t4g.micro instance with only ports 22 and 8080 open, to one IP

projects.title: Data Preparation and Statistics
projects.overview: Extends the cloud pipeline into a full cleaning and exploratory analysis workflow on SageMaker: loads the raw dataset from S3, validates and feature-engineers it with Pandas and NumPy, runs SciPy statistics, produces Matplotlib figures, and writes the cleaned dataset back to S3.
projects.learned: The missingness table was the most useful thing I produced: GRE scores were absent from over 92% of rows, which reframed every later modelling decision as a question about what applicants choose to report.
projects.highlight: 29,141 clean records from 30,000, with GRE missing in 92% of rows

projects.title: K-Means Clustering of Program Names
projects.overview: Groups inconsistently entered program names into a smaller set of program areas using TF-IDF, PCA, and K-Means, so that variants such as Business and Economics and Business Economics fall into the same cluster.
projects.learned: Picking k from an elbow plot showed me that an unsupervised result is a judgement call rather than an answer, because nothing in the data tells you the right number of clusters.
projects.highlight: 2,909 distinct program names reduced to 85 clusters

projects.title: Interactive Data Dashboard
projects.overview: An interactive Dash and Plotly dashboard asking whether LeBron James or Michael Jordan is the greater player, split into scoring peak, all-around production, and longevity, with Seaborn figures built from committed CSV snapshots so it runs with no network calls.
projects.learned: Turning one vague question into three answerable sub-questions did more for the analysis than any choice of chart type, and committing the data snapshots meant the dashboard still runs offline months later.

projects.title: MLOps Experiment Tracking
projects.overview: Wraps the Module 9 clustering pipeline in experiment tracking, logging the clustering parameters, the inertia metric, and the trained model itself to MLflow, with a flag that switches the backend to Weights and Biases.
projects.learned: Logging a run and registering the model is the difference between a script I happened to run once and an experiment I can compare against later, which is what turns a result into evidence.
projects.highlight: Inertia 7529.44 logged, model registered as Clustering version 1

projects.title: Neural Network Built from Scratch
projects.overview: A fully connected 6 to 6 to 1 neural network implemented in NumPy alone, predicting whether an applicant was accepted or rejected. The forward pass, backpropagation, loss function, and training loop are all hand written, with scikit-learn used only to split the data.
projects.learned: Deriving backpropagation by hand made the chain rule concrete in a way no framework call would have, and the honest finding was that most of the accuracy came from one feature: whether the applicant applied for a Masters or a PhD.
projects.highlight: 0.7043 test accuracy from 49 parameters, against a 0.5697 baseline

projects.title: Fine-Tuning DistilBERT and Deploying It
projects.overview: Fine-tunes a pretrained DistilBERT model on the full applicant record, free text and structured fields together, then serves it from a Will You Get In? page on the Flask site so a visitor can enter a profile and receive a prediction with a confidence score.
projects.learned: Auditing the comments field revealed that 64% of them describe the outcome rather than the applicant, so the honest accuracy is 0.7617 rather than the 0.8111 the test set reported, and that gap taught me a held-out split cannot detect a feature that quietly encodes the answer.
projects.highlight: 0.8111 test accuracy, and 0.7617 once outcome leakage is removed
